name: Latin
signature: The alphabet this book is written in: round and straight letters standing apart, with accents above (á è ê ü), a tilde (ñ) or a cedilla below (ç).
combination: A true alphabet: letters are written left to right and each spells a sound. Each language adds marks of its own to the 26 letters: accents and the diaeresis above a vowel, the tilde on ñ, the cedilla under ç, and German ß. In print every letter stands apart; a joined hand links them.
notes: The Latin-script tracks' own inventory (Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Latin): exactly the Latin characters their headwords use once decomposed (NFD): the 26 small letters, the 24 capitals in use (no X or Y), ß, œ, the precomposed ñ, á, é, í, ó, ú and ü that the cited ductus draws, the ordinal indicators ª and º, the opening marks ¿ and ¡, and seven combining marks. complete is false. Stroke order is source-gated: only rows with penLifts and strokeOrderSource carry a cited order. Letters follow the Grundschrift-App (Laborschule at Bielefeld University with the Grundschulverband; no licence, facts only), with native Spanish writers' counts from UJIpenchars2 (CC BY 4.0) as corroboration; the marks of ñ, á é í ó ú and ü, and ¿ and ¡, follow UJIpenchars2. Every path is fitted to LatinPrint-Subset.ttf, a renamed subset of SIL Global's literacy typeface Andika 7.000 (OFL-1.1), chosen because it prints the one-storey a the sources teach; the books' own text face is a different font. Rows without a source are recognition-only: strokeOrder [] means NOT VERIFIED, never none. The grave, circumflex, cedilla, macron, æ and œ have no source; ä, ö, ë, ï and ÿ would follow ü only by analogy.

strokeOrderSource.variation: The Grundschrift-App was made in a research project of the Laborschule at Bielefeld University with the Grundschulverband, on its Grundschrift school model, with a teacher advisory team. Each letter is an ordered list of paths, one per pen-down stroke, which the app makes a child trace in order. It writes the one-storey a in one stroke: anticlockwise round the bowl from the top right, back up to the top of the stem, and down the stem to the foot. The printed a joins the bowl to the stem, so the path runs back up the stem to its top before it comes down, as the source does. UJIpenchars2 (Prat, Castro, Llorens, Marzal and Vilar; UCI Machine Learning Repository dataset 177, CC BY 4.0) holds 120 tablet pen traces of a, two by each of 60 adult Spanish writers; only counts are cited. 118 of the 120 are one stroke, the source's count; 92 of those 118 start at the top (72 top centre, 20 top right), and 111 go anticlockwise round the bowl. The app's repository has no licence, so only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from it; no point is copied, and the path is fitted to the a of the bundled LatinPrint-Subset.ttf, a renamed subset of SIL Global's literacy typeface Andika 7.000, which prints the one-storey a the school model teaches; the book's own text face is a different font. Handwriting varies by writer.

marks.attachesAs: a short stroke above, falling to the right: an open è (French, Italian), a stressed final vowel (Italian città), the contraction à (Portuguese)
a short stroke above, rising to the right: the stressed vowel (Spanish, Portuguese, Italian) or a closed é (French)
a small roof above: a closed vowel (Portuguese ê, ô) or a lost letter (French forêt)
a small wave above: Spanish ñ (ny), a nasal vowel in Portuguese (ã, õ)
a short bar above: a long vowel (Latin ā ē ī ō ū)
two dots above: German ä ö ü, or a vowel said apart from the one before it (French ï ë)
a small hook below: ç says s before a, o or u (French, Portuguese)
